title: Validating GPU Platforms with Runtime AI Inventory via the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory | NVIDIA Technical Blog
gist: NVIDIA's open source AI Cluster Runtime (AICR), part of the DSX AI Factory Platform, now qualifies Google's k8s-aibom to emit CycloneDX 1.6 AI bills of materials for AI workloads on GPU Kubernetes (initially H100 on GKE), pairing validated platform configuration with runtime workload inventory. The tutorial stresses that signing, verified provenance and intent-vs-observed correlation remain future work.

insights.claim: NVIDIA AI Cluster Runtime (AICR), an open source component of the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform, now ships a qualified AI bill of materials (AIBOM) component built on Google's open source k8s-aibom project to track AI workloads running on Kubernetes.
insights.speaker: Mark Chmarny
insights.so_what: NVIDIA and Google are co-building open governance tooling around GPU Kubernetes stacks, deepening NVIDIA's software lock-in at the AI-factory layer beyond the GPU itself.
insights.quote: An open source project created by Google, k8s-aibom tracks AI workloads running on Kubernetes.
insights.locator: NVIDIA AI Cluster Runtime (AICR), an open source

insights.claim: NVIDIA's AICR stock recipes h100-gke-cos-inference and h100-gke-cos-inference-dynamo select k8s-aibom by default, while other GKE recipes can opt in with the --runtime-inventory flag; the initial integration is scoped to H100 GPUs on Google Kubernetes Engine.
insights.speaker: Mark Chmarny
insights.so_what: The first qualified path is GKE + H100, signalling Google Cloud as a preferred launch partner for NVIDIA's AI-factory software stack.
insights.locator: Two stock recipes select k8s-aibom by default

insights.claim: NVIDIA's AICR turns known-good GPU platform configurations into version-locked recipes and reproducible deployment bundles, each recipe pinning components, versions, constraints, ordering and validation expectations for one hardware/cloud/OS/intent combination.
insights.speaker: Mark Chmarny
insights.so_what: Reproducible, validated GPU-cluster configs reduce deployment friction for enterprises and neoclouds, extending NVIDIA's control over the full stack from drivers to Kubernetes.
insights.locator: AICR turns known-good GPU platform configurations

insights.claim: NVIDIA frames AICR qualification of k8s-aibom as more than a rubber stamp: it binds the exact upstream source, chart, CRDs and digest-pinned controller image as one tested set and verifies provenance against Google's expected build identity.
insights.speaker: Mark Chmarny
insights.so_what: Supply-chain provenance is becoming a selling point for AI infrastructure software; NVIDIA positions itself as the curator/qualifier of the open source stack.
insights.quote: Qualification with k8s-aibom is a specific claim, not a rubber stamp.
insights.locator: Qualification with k8s-aibom is a specific

themes.theme: Governance gap: config vs. running workloads

insights.claim: A reproducible GPU platform deployment bundle cannot establish which AI workload artifacts are actually running on each node, because application teams update workloads independently of the platform recipe, and mutable image tags like :latest let two nodes run different code under identical tags.
insights.speaker: Mark Chmarny
insights.so_what: Shadow and drifting AI workloads are a real enterprise security/compliance gap, creating demand for AI-specific inventory and governance tooling.
insights.quote: Two nodes can end up running different code under identical tags
insights.locator: As teams deploy and scale AI workloads

insights.claim: NVIDIA argues neither platform-configuration validation (AICR) nor runtime workload observation (k8s-aibom) is sufficient for AI governance on its own, and that the boundary between the two is where accountability is currently missing.
insights.speaker: Mark Chmarny
insights.so_what: AI governance/compliance is an emerging software category; vendors bridging infra intent and runtime observation stand to capture it.
insights.quote: the boundary between them is exactly where accountability is missing today
insights.locator: Both projects arrived at this from opposite

insights.claim: An AIBOM differs from a conventional SBOM by identifying which model is serving and which runtime serves it, not just which container image runs; k8s-aibom emits CycloneDX 1.6 AIBOM records with four confidence tiers (declared, inferred, unresolved, verified) plus evidence locators.
insights.speaker: Mark Chmarny
insights.so_what: AIBOM as a standard artifact (CycloneDX 1.6) could become a compliance requirement, benefiting security/supply-chain tooling vendors.
insights.quote: A conventional SBOM tells you which image is running. An AIBOM tells you which model is serving and which runtime is serving it.
insights.locator: A conventional SBOM tells you which image

insights.claim: k8s-aibom is pitched to find unregistered or shadow AI workloads, identify models, inference runtimes, agents and RAG components, track external AI APIs and vector databases, and detect drift in AI dependencies for security reviews and compliance audits.
insights.speaker: Mark Chmarny
insights.so_what: Enterprise AI sprawl (agents, RAG, external APIs) is now visible enough that inventory tooling is being productized at the infrastructure layer.
insights.locator: Find unregistered or shadow AI workloads

insights.claim: k8s-aibom inventories only supported workload kinds carrying a recognized AI signal, including native NVIDIA Dynamo graphs, NIMService, LeaderWorkerSet, DisaggregatedSet and CronJob resources; in a demo it auto-classified a vLLM deployment serving Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct as an inference workload on the vllm runtime.
insights.speaker: Mark Chmarny
insights.so_what: First-class support for NVIDIA Dynamo and NIM in the inventory reinforces NVIDIA's serving software as the default path on Kubernetes.
insights.locator: k8s-aibom looks higher up the stack

insights.claim: An AIBOM record is built from the workload spec, so it can exist and report Ready=True before any pod runs; it records what was declared and resolved but does not prove successful scheduling or execution.
insights.speaker: Mark Chmarny
insights.so_what: Buyers should not treat AIBOM as proof of runtime state — a limitation that leaves room for complementary attestation and observability products.
insights.quote: It does not prove successful scheduling or execution.
insights.locator: The controller automatically classified the workload

insights.claim: Upstream measurements of k8s-aibom v1.6.1 on GKE showed roughly four API-server requests per minute, 2.2 millicores average controller CPU and a 28–34 MiB memory working set over a 15-minute steady-state window (on CPU-only nodes with pending workload pods).
insights.speaker: Mark Chmarny
insights.so_what: Negligible overhead lowers adoption barriers for AI inventory on production GPU clusters.

insights.claim: The AICR–k8s-aibom integration deliberately leaves runtime AIBOM observations unsigned, keeps k8s-aibom's Sigstore/Rekor model-signature verification disabled by default, and treats correlating AICR deployment intent with observed workloads as future integration work.
insights.speaker: Mark Chmarny
insights.so_what: Signed, end-to-end AI provenance (platform attestation linked to runtime inventory) is the next step to watch; it is not yet delivered.
insights.quote: The integration deliberately stops short of a few things, each its own decision rather than an oversight.
